exportTitle: Closing the Gap: How a Fairer Global Economy Could Lift Billions
exportSummary: Imagine a World Where Progress Doesn’t Leave People Behind
title: The Distribution Myth
subtitle: In a system flooded with wealth, fairness remains an accounting illusion.
seriesLine: A Ledger Series article on fairness, inequality, and the illusion of equal access.
summary: Imagine a World Where Progress Doesn’t Leave People Behind
description: Imagine a World Where Progress Doesn’t Leave People Behind
author: Tai Song

children.text: A software developer in Germany and a factory worker in Bangladesh both show up to work every day. One earns more in a week than the other does in a year. One has access to free healthcare, social safety nets, and robust digital infrastructure. The other faces power outages, limited internet access, and rising food prices.
The difference isn’t talent. It isn’t effort.
It’s the system.
Despite global advances in technology, production, and wealth, over 3 billion people still live on less than $6.85 a day. (
worldbank.org
) Meanwhile, the richest 10% hold nearly 75% of the world’s total wealth. (
wid.world
We often talk about inequality within countries. But the biggest divides today are between them.

This article explores how the global economy still favors the wealthiest nations, and how that could change. Not through charity, but through new trade policies, debt reform, infrastructure investment, and digital inclusion.
The tools to close the gap already exist. The question is: do we want a global economy that works for everyone, or just for a few?
The Geography of Inequality
The global economy doesn’t operate on a level playing field, and the numbers make that painfully clear.
Income Gaps:
As of 2023, the average GDP per capita in North America is over $70,000. In Sub-Saharan Africa, it’s just above $1,700. (
worldbank.org
) In some low-income countries, a full-time job doesn’t guarantee enough to meet basic needs.
Education Access:

Children in wealthier countries have access to quality public education, free school meals, and internet in classrooms. In many parts of the Global South, schools lack electricity, teachers are underpaid, and girls drop out early due to household responsibilities or safety concerns.
Healthcare Inequality:
A child born in Japan can expect to live 84 years. In Chad, life expectancy is 53. (
worldbank.org
) One country has universal healthcare and elder care. The other struggles with clean water access.
Digital Divide:

Roughly one in three people worldwide still lack reliable internet access. Without connectivity, there’s no access to digital education, remote work, or e-commerce. The divide isn’t just technological, it’s economic.
These disparities didn’t happen by accident. They’re the result of centuries of unequal development, resource extraction, and policies that have reinforced a two-tier global economy.
But it doesn’t have to stay that way.
Where the System Fails
Many low and middle-income countries aren’t struggling because they lack effort or ideas. They’re stuck in global systems that were never designed for their success.
Debt Before Development
As of 2023, developing countries paid a record $1.4 trillion to service their foreign debt as their interest costs climbed to a 20-year high. (
worldbank.org
) Many of these debts were taken decades ago under poor terms, and the interest just keeps growing. Even in the face of climate disasters or pandemics, repayments come first.
Unfair Trade Rules
Africa accounts for less than 3% of global trade. (
worldbank.org

) High tariffs, export quotas, and subsidies in the Global North make it hard for farmers and small manufacturers to access markets. A tomato grower in Ghana can’t compete with a subsidized EU producer. The playing field is tilted.
Brain Drain

Many of the brightest minds in lower-income countries leave to study or work abroad , and don’t come back. That’s not a failure of ambition. It’s a lack of opportunity at home. Countries invest in education, but richer nations reap the rewards.
Extraction Without Investment

Natural resources from Latin America, Asia, and Africa fuel industries in wealthier countries. But local communities often see little benefit. Profits go abroad. Infrastructure is minimal. And once the mines or oil fields are dry, companies move on.
These are not isolated problems. They’re signs of a global economic system that rewards power, not fairness.
But there are real, evidence-based ways to change that.
What a Fairer Global Economy Looks Like
A global economy that works for everyone isn’t about handouts. It’s about redesigning systems to support long-term, shared prosperity.
Debt Relief with Conditions That Build, Not Punish

Instead of austerity, debt restructuring could be tied to investments in health, education, and clean energy. Programs like the IMF’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust are steps in this direction, but they need to be bigger, faster, and more inclusive.
Open and Equitable Trade Access

Trade agreements should lower barriers for lower-income countries, not protect corporate interests. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is a powerful start, creating the world’s largest free trade zone by population. But it needs global cooperation to succeed.
Investment in Infrastructure, Not Just Aid

Digital infrastructure, sustainable transport, and renewable energy are the foundations of modern economies. Investing in these isn’t charity, it’s smart economics. For every $1 invested in infrastructure, the World Bank estimates up to $4 in economic return.
Technology Transfer and Fair Taxation

Multinational tech companies operate globally but often pay minimal tax in the countries they profit from. New global tax frameworks and open-access tech initiatives can shift this dynamic, so innovation benefits all, not just the few.
Support for Local Industry and Innovation

From fintech startups in Kenya to green energy firms in Bangladesh, innovation is happening everywhere. Fair financing and IP reform can ensure these ideas scale globally, without being swallowed by monopolies.
This isn’t idealism. It’s policy, and it’s already working in places that have tried it.
Rising Together: Why It’s Not Just Charity
Helping lower-income countries grow isn’t a moral obligation alone, it’s in everyone’s best interest.
A Stronger Global Economy
More economic equality means more demand, more trade, and more innovation. When billions of people gain access to education, tools, and capital, global markets expand. Everyone benefits.
Less Instability, More Security

Poverty and inequality fuel conflict, displacement, and political unrest. A more balanced global economy reduces the drivers of war and forced migration, making the world safer and more stable for all.
A Bigger Innovation Base
Talent is everywhere, but opportunity is not. When more countries have the infrastructure to support science, technology, and entrepreneurship, humanity as a whole moves faster.
Real Partnerships, Not Dependence
Empowering countries to build resilient local economies leads to long-term collaboration, not dependency. It shifts the narrative from “aid” to “investment in shared progress.”
This is the opportunity: a shift from extraction to cooperation. Not just to do what’s fair, but to do what works.
The Choice Ahead
The global economy has lifted millions, but it has left billions behind. We now have the data, tools, and technology to change that. What’s missing is the decision to act.
Left as-is, the current system will keep rewarding wealth, not need. Inequality will grow. Instability will rise. And opportunities will continue to cluster in the same corners of the world.
But we can choose differently.
We can rewrite trade rules, restructure debt, invest in connectivity, and design policies that include, not exclude. We can build a global economy based not on extraction, but on shared potential.
This isn’t about lowering anyone’s quality of life. It’s about raising the global floor so that every country, no matter its past, has a fair shot at the future.
Do you think a more equal global economy is possible?
What would it take for every country to thrive, not just survive?
Drop your thoughts in the comments. Let’s reimagine what global progress could look like together.
